speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head V of the Estimates be reduced by $100." As a small and open economy, Singapore can only be a price taker in the global marketplace realistically.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Staying competitive is a given but that just puts you in the starting line.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to develop both value-adding capabilities, which I will touch on later, and, equally important, our market connectivity capabilities, so that we can sell our products and services to the consumers of the world.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Having both sets of capabilities and the intensity of them will determine how much of a livelihood we can make for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Singapore's context, staying open and connected to the world is key and our only pathway to continued economic growth and progress.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today, our international linkages and market connectivity enable us to transcend our limited domestic market and create for ourselves a bigger hinterland to operate in.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to continually expand and upgrade our network of trade partnerships and investment agreements so that our companies can not only have a bigger economic space to do business in but are also able to ride on the growth and opportunities in the emerging markets.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Over the decades, we have done very well to strengthen our air, sea and land connectivity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the new landscape, we need to develop other new sets of connectivities, such as regulations, data, talent, finance and technology.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These efforts are primarily Government-driven but, importantly, we also need businesses to step up to seize these opportunities from the enhanced connectivity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It requires the companies to build up the required capabilities to internationalise both at the enterprise and the workforce levels.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Capabilities, such as deep understanding of the target markets, ability to mobilise and deploy resources and talents across markets and jurisdictions, ability to obtain local funding and manage currency risks, among others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our economic agencies already provide both financial and non-financial support to help companies internationalise, such as in in-market landing pads, overseas centres and so on.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here, I would like to ask the Minister if the support has been adequate and has there been good traction.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Beyond the more familiar markets like China, India and the developed economies, do our economic agencies need to step up expertise and presence in newer and more frontier markets as we know that these markets tend to have less developed market data and a more challenging regulatory and operating environment?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can the Trade Associations and Chambers (TACs) play an enabling role to help businesses seeking to internationalise, especially in less familiar markets?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On diversification of international markets, the COVID-19 outbreak reminded us on the urgency to seek more and newer markets, especially in emerging economies and to minimise concentration risk on any single market.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even without the COVID-19 outbreak, global supply chains are already showing signs of disruptions and are likely to be reorganised.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can we help our companies diversify their markets and adjust to the shift in supply chains to increase business resilience?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Next, and still related to diversifying our economy, I would like to seek an update from the Minister on the progress of building new economic clusters.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, how have we leveraged the technological advancements to open up possibilities in new sectors?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Beyond agri-tech and sustainability solutions, are there more new growth sectors that we are developing?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Continued rapid advancements in technology are likely to add to further disruptions and even lead to the demise of some sectors.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to open up new industries and growth sectors to keep generating the positive deltas to our economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fostering new economic growth sectors can also help create new and more exciting jobs and it can help boost the overall productivity and innovations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We know that investing into new growth sectors carry significant investment risks.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It requires sectoral expertise and talents, it requires products that meet the addressable markets, the necessary ecosystem players and, importantly, the entrepreneurial acumen and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can the Government facilitate the development of new growth sectors and the necessary ecosystems?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What are the resources and support to be provided?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Budget 2020, the Finance Minister also mentioned about improving support for deep-tech startups.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can the Minister also share on how the Government plans to nurture and help promising startups?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Given this diverse enterprise landscape, a one-size-fits-all approach may not meet the specific needs and achieve the desired outcomes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How could our economic agencies work with the relevant stakeholders to provide differentiated support for different types of companies?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A pro-enterprise environment is also a necessary condition for a vibrant and entrepreneurial ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Is there scope to adopt a light-touch approach in regulations so as to encourage more enterprises to innovate and venture?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Having employers take ownership in developing their staff is the most ideal situation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The companies know best the skills needed for their businesses to grow and transform.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The employers are in the best position to manage the resources, time and space to upgrade skills.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They are also in the vantage position to plan out and execute job redesign, which can align the necessary training and reskilling to the business need.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is the most tangible move to date by the Government to help mid-career Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Employers should leverage this reskilling programme to help enhance their workforce and yet also enjoy the wage support.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I call on employers to discard any age biases that they may have in their human resource (HR) policy and re-pivot to the new environment of higher retirement age.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The first wave impact to our affected businesses, such as tourism, aviation and retail, has been very sharp and severe.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, I am concerned that if this COVID-19 situation is prolonged, we may lose capabilities and capacities in the tourism sectors as operators may downsize or shut their operations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I hope that the Government would monitor this closely and be ready to extend and step up the assistance further.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Given the severity of the outbreak in China, its economy is likely to take a major hit.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If the situation persists, its production capacity would be curtailed and we could see serious disruption to the supply chain and this has wider and deeper implication and impact on the world's trade flows.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On the demand side, slower growth in China is also expected to dampen consumption and investments.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore, like many economies, is unlikely to be spared from the further knock-on effects.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can we draw lessons from the impact of COVID-19 to build economic and national resilience?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Teo Ser Luck, you have three cuts.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our economic growth is getting more and more challenging.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Each year, as we forecast our economic growth, you will realise that we keep revising our forecast.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: From last year to this year, we are revising downwards on the forecast.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is challenging, no doubt, and, with COVID-19, it is getting more and more challenging to actually get a part of the pie because other cities and economies are also getting more competitive.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We are focusing on quite a few verticals and I know that we rely less on manufacturing now, which, in the past, was about 25% contribution to GDP.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But right now, we are looking at 20% GDP.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Although there is a lot of focus on precision engineering and some of the rest of the other sectors related to manufacturing, for the long haul, it does not give as much stimulating growth to the economy as we need.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, that is why we are investing in technology startups or we are investing in financial services and all.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, for some of this growth, we are competing very intensively with other economies as well and that will pose a challenge to our economic growth as a whole.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the 23 Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs) that we have focused on, I do not think we can focus on all 23.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But what are the key focuses that we can have in order to boost the economy forward, maybe the next three to five years of economic growth that can be greater than 3%?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Because we have not seen anything before with 5% to 8% anymore.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What are the other measures that we can put in?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With COVID-19, I was wondering whether the Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) can play a part?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: FTAs, in good times, actually help the small and medium enterprises (SMEs), which understood FTAs and can launch their products overseas and get the full benefits out of them – tax incentives and other measures in regulations, in actually getting exceptions.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One of the most practical methods for businesses in Singapore to actually overcome some of these challenges, for example, some of the crises that we faced today and some of the growth challenges, will actually be using some of the schemes that we have.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The important thing about launching businesses overseas is, firstly, the regulations; secondly, the knowledge on the legal aspect, the framework; thirdly, it is finding a local partnership.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Sometimes, it is not about funds, because MRA provides the funds.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But it is the knowledge that is the most important.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can MRA offer more than just funds, dollars and cents, but actually coming in with certain knowledge?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Because we have Enterprise Singapore (ESG) officers all over internationally and they are very good officers.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They can provide their facilitation of good help and networking.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Douglas Foo, you have two cuts, take both together, please.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, ASEAN is widely seen to be on track to be the 4th largest economy in the world by 2030.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This is driven by the continued economic growth and development efforts of our neighbours.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: ASEAN is an incredibly dynamic economic block with 10 economies at different stages of development.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As the world embarks on a new decade with uncertainty as the opening number, this is a turning point for ASEAN to realise our ambition to be the next "factory of the world".

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: There is definitely opportunity to attract foreign interest in ASEAN in the current uncertain global trade climate.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, our member states need to encourage our companies to reinvest in the region to further spur on growth.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In our recent dialogues with members in the manufacturing community, in view of the current supply chain challenges arising from the COVID-19 outbreak, more businesses are seeking to explore longer-term solutions for their businesses in ASEAN countries.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This provides the impetus for Singapore businesses to take a closer look at the opportunities in ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As we continue ground efforts like leading mission trips and business meetings, are there any additional outreach or publicity efforts that will be undertaken by the Ministry to continue to highlight to businesses the importance and promise of our ASEAN neighbours?

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Because at the end of the day, by 2030, when we look back, we want our enterprises to have actually ridden the journey of ASEAN having risen to being the fourth largest economy in the world.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, answering the call by the Government, Trade Association and Chambers (TACs) have stepped up to play a much larger role in outreach and capability-building in the business community.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Within TACs, there is also a higher level of collaboration to collectively address key business issues.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The TAC leaders had the opportunity to engage in a dialogue with Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance Heng Swee Keat.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: During this session, the TACs deep dived into pertinent issues, such as internationalisation, innovation and digitalisation, as well as how TACs need to transform to stay relevant for the future.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As noted by Mr Ho Meng Kit, the Chief Executive Officer of SBF, "with more complex challenges faced by our members, TACs need to change, adapt and innovate to better serve the community.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As we continue to take on bigger roles, TACs are also beginning to face a number of operational challenges".

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In the circumstances, how does the Ministry intend to encourage TACs to pool knowledge and resources together both locally and in overseas markets to help businesses seeking to internationalise?

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Does the Ministry have any plans to assist TACs to upgrade their capabilities and human talent and make this a possible career choice for the workforce?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Mr Chairman, there are many grants and schemes which are available to help companies.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Now, these have been made available by the Government through various agencies to encourage a vibrant business community in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: However, many companies, particularly SMEs, are often not aware of the grants available to them.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Or if they know of these grants, the amount of red tape and the number of forms they need to fill in could also prove to be an impediment to applying for these schemes.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Or there may be multiple overlapping and similar schemes, and it is hard for a business owner to decide which one to apply for.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: I am sure not many SMEs know of the existence of SME Centres, which have been specifically set up to help them.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: While SME Centres will be able to help SMEs navigate the various grants and schemes which are available, they may not be visible enough for the SMEs, such that SMEs actually reach out to them to tap on their expertise.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: More broadly, is the Minister satisfied that the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) is doing enough to ensure that SMEs are made aware of the grants, schemes and programmes available to them, and could more be done to ensure that SMEs do not lose out on these?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Implemented well, FTAs can introduce a wider range of goods and services in Singapore at lower prices for the end consumer while also giving our local firms greater market access and a more level playing field abroad.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is feedback gathered from local firms as to the analysis of prices of goods and services before and after?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is that kind of analysis done, for example?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Chairman, the COVID-19 situation is an unpleasant but timely reminder of the importance of diversification.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is dangerous to develop a reliance on one market.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: China has been an excellent trading partner with a vast market, offering generous business opportunities for Singaporeans across a wide variety of sectors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But with China taking a significant hit, many local businesses are also reeling from the impact.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, it is crucial they set their sights on the broader horizon and work towards them or risk sinking.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, for companies entering a new market, and especially for those who are new to internationalisation efforts, they would feel quite lost and may not even know what they can do with the funding.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: TACs have been playing increasingly critical roles in driving transformation and growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Being close to the ground, they have a firm grasp of their members’ needs and a greater understanding of the industry.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They have in recent years helped their members to adopt new innovative solutions and technologies to transform their businesses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They have also worked closely with the Government to help members.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is evident that they will, and must continue, to take on integral positions in this next round of internationalisation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Chairman, in the midst of this uncertain economy, our mature and mid-career workers, many in their 40s and 50s, are most vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the recent economic challenges and rapid technological advancement, some of them are struggling to make their career transitions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I wish to acknowledge their efforts to make use of SkillsFuture and other excellent Government initiatives to reskill themselves.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For every successful story, another shares his failed attempts to secure a good job despite months of networking, attending courses, seeking career guidance and so on.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope the Minister will share with us further efforts to grow the economy and how this will translate into good jobs and outcomes for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In recent years, aviation, food and beverage, retail and tourism were booming.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They were among the major sectors offering Professional Conversion Programme (PCP) and other mid-career transition measures.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Today, Government support is needed to help these industries tide over difficult times.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have confidence that this is only temporary and they will bounce back in good time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But for those who have made the transition or are in the midst of getting the relevant qualifications and training to enter these industries, I wonder if their employment prospects will be affected.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Yet, such global crises are impossible to predict.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What else will be done to help workers remain employable and industry-relevant in the rapidly changing environment?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am glad that the Deputy Prime Minister reinforced his resolution in the Budget to move away from reliance on the foreign workforce.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, there must also be greater effort and localisation efforts to support Singapore's competitiveness and worker sustainability.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This can be targeted for a range of skills and may need to be company-specific or dependent.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It could be, for example, incorporating elements of training for eventual local employment and with a specific localisation target, for example, in three to five years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The existing CTP supports firms to bring in foreign specialists to transfer capabilities to the local workforce, and to send locals abroad for training.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The foreign specialists that they bring in should mentor Singaporeans to take over or share the role.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can we also consider CTP to support transfer of capabilities from foreign employees already employed in Singapore to local workers, with the eventual aim of localising jobs, working in tandem with the localisation targets I had mentioned earlier?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Chairman, in the face of significant economic and technology shifts, upskilling and reskilling are paramount to good employment outcomes for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: One can argue that success in both of these areas are some of the hardest public policy that few governments have succeeded in.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There are several reasons and it is a complex issue.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Successful upskilling is usually done by successful companies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Because successful companies are the ones who have a clear vision for the future, and therefore the skills needed to reach that future.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: They are also usually operating within a certain national culture, such as those found in Germany and Japan, where companies have a firm sense of responsibility to the long-term employment of the staff.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This culture is usually supported by manpower policy at the national level.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Upskilling also requires complementary educational institutes and capability for both full-time and part-time upskilling.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: If upskilling is difficult, reskilling could be even more challenging.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, one would be stretched to think about more than a handful of countries that had systematically reskilled people who are structurally unemployed.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Reskilling workers to do different jobs is somewhat easier for larger companies, because while they are learning these new skills, they are usually working within the same company, within the culture.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, as DBS banks digitise, many of its frontline workers got a place to be retrained within other parts of the bank.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: However, it is not always so easy to reskill these people across the broader economy, because not many companies have the scale like DBS.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Because in the interconnected world, international companies have the option of relocating jobs outside Singapore, rather than reskilling our workers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Because in this age of technology disruption, not all industries have a strong awareness of what is coming ahead and, therefore, workers who are currently within or are trying to enter that industry may not know what skills to reskill on.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, how can we upskill more workers in industry-relevant competencies, such as in the area of design?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The mindset of our workers is also pivotal.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: They must understand that in this day and age, careers are non-linear, and they must upskill and reskill themselves multiple times through their career.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And how is the Government publicising such information in a systematic manner?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: COVID-19 outbreak has caused economic weaknesses and companies might be putting off the transformation work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Which are the industries that the Ministry expects to experience a longer recovery time?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How is the Ministry helping these industries to continue the transformation?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: According to some SME bosses, during a downturn, it is also the best time to transform.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But the realities of a rapidly changing economy are unchanging.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How is the Ministry helping these companies to accelerate workforce transformation?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Transformation would inevitably cause some of our workers to be left behind.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is especially acute amongst those in their 40s and 50s.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How is the Ministry helping to keep them employable and industry-relevant?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many companies are reluctant to train because the workers might be poached.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This mindset is perhaps the greatest obstacle to manpower transformation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Amazon pays 95% of education fees and work flexibility for workers to pick up skills in industries that are in demand and well-paid, regardless of whether those skills are relevant to Amazon or not.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Amazon possibly gains because it is seen as a progressive company.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It can possibly only retain the promising ones.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The industry and broader economy gain from the more-skilled workers, and workers gain by better skills, better jobs and wages.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have many large companies in Singapore that have accumulated vast resources over time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If enough of them follow Amazon's example, it need not be a zero-sum game of one company producing better skilled workers for others to poach.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can, in fact, grow the pie so that we can grow and benefit our workers collectively.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Going forward, it is important to support and develop Singaporean leaders in the private sector.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: To the extent that there are impediments to this, these should be understood and addressed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What has been the success associated with such programmes to date?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: The question I have is that I do see many other related Ministries or relevant Ministries also putting in some of the investments into startups and also into technology.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: The question I have is whether there is synergy between them.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: And when we put in additional funds into it, what are the key performance indicators or indicators of success for such funds?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: I do not think we can compare a public fund for such investments like the private funds where their return on investments (ROIs) is in terms of the immediate returns or short-term returns.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: But what exactly would be the indicator of success for our funds?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: The question is that their success is dependent on the commercialisation aspect of these startups because you do not want to invest in startups where it is just another science project.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: If it is another science project, then you come out of the lab but there is no commercial value, there is no demand.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: We have to put in some of these funds, for example, the $300 million additional funds, put them into agri-tech.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Would the agri-tech in future provide a more comparative and affordable pricing for some of what it produces, or these technology startups would be able to scale overseas globally and have a commercial aspect to that?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: I would like the Ministry to be able to elaborate further on what indicators are there for such an assessment.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore’s investment in economic transformation seems to be moving in the right direction.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The ITMs aimed at fostering innovation, boosting productivity and deepening skills of workers in the respective industries are central to our economic restructuring effort.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Yet, when I speak to business leaders, they continue to lament that potential synergies and capability development which ITMs could provide, remain under-leveraged.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Performance in industry transformation has been uneven across sectors.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister what lessons have been gleaned from the implementation of ITMs thus far.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How can companies be better incentivised to band together and form alliances to develop industry-wide capabilities, build scale, go international and test sector-wide solutions?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: What progress has been made in the Government’s efforts to anchor key players in shared facilities and infrastructure to better support transformation and adoption of technology?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: And lastly, how can the Government support the development of emerging sectors with good growth potential?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For example, what can we learn from manufacturers in the semiconductor and pharmaceutical industries who have widely been recognised as the forerunners in the adoption of Industry 4.0 initiatives?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: SMEs need a lot of handholding to engage in research and development (R&D).

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: What impact has the 10 Centres of Innovation (COIs) had on industry development?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: What outcomes have there been so far of COIs in assisting SMEs?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: And how can university research and other research agencies support industry development in more substantive ways?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As Singapore is now also a globally recognised leader of IP protection and scientific research centre, we should fully deploy our strengths to focus on supporting startups in deep-tech with research-based IP at its core.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, I would like to ask the Government how are we going to support these startups.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, 5G, robotics and so on are poised to shape future industries.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The emergence of Industry 4.0 and Services 4.0, are fast becoming the new global landscape.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: In fact, the ongoing technology boom shows no signs of slowing.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Here in Singapore, many companies are trying to automate their operations without hiring more workers.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: While Singapore is making all efforts to transform, we may still be too slow for competition.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Against this backdrop, I would like to ask the Minister, how has MTI been preparing our enterprises and workforce to adjust to the new economic landscape?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: In leading sectors, such as AI and Blockchain, where we are short of a critical mass of talents and companies to play in the global game, have MTI agencies made concerted efforts to bring in lead players and top talents to catalyse our local ecosystem development?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Given that the Chinese economy is now the second largest, and several of their information technology (IT) and digital sectors are world-leading, has MTI been successful in attracting Chinese unicorns to be located in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: How is MTI going to identify and attract would-be unicorns from China, India and ASEAN so that Singapore has a fair share of the future Asia unicorns, going forward?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Leon Perera, you can take both your cuts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, the challenge of navigating Industry 4.0 is all about attracting investments in future-ready categories like AI, drones, Internet-of-Things (IoT) and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But that, in turn, can be unpacked into several distinct challenges that need to be met to attract that investment.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: While investments in Singapore would be to serve the region and the world, some local demand would help attract the attention of investors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Fourthly, creating network effects where interactions among players and industry, academia, research centres, Government and top leaders can take place, thus catalysing new ideas.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: To address the fourth challenge, why not catalyse the creation of networking platforms for distinct Industry 4.0 spaces like AI and IoT?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: One useful model could be the Product Executive Forum in Boston, an exclusive group for senior product leaders in that area.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It brings together promising industry executives, academics and top leaders.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It functions through breakfast seminars, roundtables and other events.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: After all, in the Industry 4.0 race, it is not just about having the right people but also about those people interacting and cross-fertilising ideas and work streams.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, natural gas is the main way Singapore generates its electricity today.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It was not too clear if pipeline gas from Natunas would be similarly affected but the statement emanating from Indonesia's Energy and Mineral Resources Ministry on 8 February would seem to suggest so.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If this takes place, it will place some pressure on our power-generation sources.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Renewable energy sources, mainly solar power, as well as regional power grids, would take time to build up.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Would the Government share its mitigation measures in light of this?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Can LNG imports, for example, plug any gap that emerges after 2023?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We should also take this opportunity to improve the renewable portion of our power generation mix.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I am heartened to hear about the decarbonisation measures spoken about by the Government in Parliament last week.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My colleague, Mr Dennis Tan, outlined various perspectives and suggestions from the Workers' Party on environmental policy in his Budget speech last week.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Russia and China are exploring floating nuclear power plants based on seaborne platforms, with Russia in the process of deploying one.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It may or may not be a practical possibility for Singapore to derive power by such means in the foreseeable future.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But is the Government studying the risks that such projects by other countries may pose to Singapore?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Ministry consider (a) conducting and publishing stress test exercises specific to the petrochemical industry to understand growth risk under different scenarios of global carbon policy; (b) evaluating the potential for job creation, cost of living and environmental impact around carbon capture and storage, solar photovoltaic, nuclear, importing renewable energy, increasing industrial energy efficiency; and (c) developing a clear plan of economic transition to reduce our reliance on high carbon risk sectors, including actively involving our oil and gas industry before 2030?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Chairman, let me begin by declaring that I am a senior executive with an industrial gas and engineering company.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The physical effects of climate change are increasingly visible on the environment, society and the global economy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Climate change is not a distant threat; it is happening now.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Increasingly, people want to know if you are part of the problem or part of the solution.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: There has been much discussion on emission reductions focused primarily on high carbon footprint industries, specifically the petrochemical and manufacturing industries.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Before we focus on any individual, we must first put in perspective and recognise there are many parts in the entire value chain before the GHG emissions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But hydrogen is an essential ingredient to produce low-sulfur fuels to meet even stricter environmental standards, thereby reducing the sulfur emissions into our environment.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Hydrogen technology can also be used as a transformative energy carrier or as clean fuel for mobility and transportation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is important to understand whether the products being produced, the manufacturing processes used and the industry value chain on the whole actually have a larger benefit to the society in terms of carbon productivity, support sustainability and how they help to avoid more GHG emissions on a net basis.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Further, we have to ask if the industries invest in new technologies that drive operational efficiency, thereby reducing GHG, adopt usage of renewable energy sources in their production that shape the energy transformation, reuse the waste streams or capture the carbon emitted for alternate usage.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Whether the industries are working towards decarbonisation that contributes towards managing climate change is key.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Planning and facilitating transitions towards "cleaner" modes of operation and to cleaner industries would result in significant economic impact in terms of jobs, cost and overall operations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: No industry is spared from the effects of climate change and all sectors have to play their part in mitigating the effects of climate change.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Through this, companies can harness the best knowledge, balance their obligations to all stakeholders to continue driving their financial performance while being a good steward of our environment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, the Government has implemented many policies to boost productivity growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Recent schemes include the Productivity Solutions Grant, Enterprise Development Grant and Automation Support Package.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2020's Transformation and Growth strategies continue these efforts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: How effective are each of the recent productivity growth grant schemes in terms of the marginal return to public spending and the impact on industry and jobs?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: To what extent can we attribute recent improvements in Total Factor Productivity growth to these policies?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: MTI's Economist Service publishes excellent research on the effects of various industry policies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Each scheme should have a logic model that defines target outcomes prior to implementation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Evaluation results should be published at clear intervals, such as at the mid-term and shortly after the conclusion of the scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The most important schemes should have their evaluation results subjected to academic peer review to enhance credibility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Technology-driven innovation can improve productivity, worker welfare and make jobs more desirable to Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In a recent working paper, Prof Ivan Png from the National University of Singapore studied a supermarket chain in Singapore that redesigned the cashier's job to focus only on scanning groceries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Switching to a scan-only job format improved worker welfare and boosted local recruitment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Prof Png's research highlights the importance of carefully scrutinising the effects of technology improvements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We should not spend such significant sums on productivity transformation without an equally strong commitment to understanding whether such efforts are cost-effective and meaningful.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: SMEs form an integral part of our economy and are seen as the future drivers of Singapore's growth.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: With the number of SMEs constantly hovering at above 200,000 companies, there is, understandably, a wide range of companies all at very different stages of growth.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: While there is a host of support for startups and small SMEs, understandably which are more vulnerable, it is timely that we look into investing and supporting SMEs which have managed to show a good track record and are ready to embark on the next stage of growth.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: With the announcement of the Enterprise Leadership for Transformation Programme as part of the Enterprise Transform Package, I believe this is a good extension of our current SME support framework.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: SMF stands ready to assist to reach out to this community.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: I strongly believe that TACs can be a useful platform to reach out to these business leaders and engage them with new initiatives, such as this.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: With its aim as providing training to business leaders, the Enterprise Leadership for Transformation Programme is one for the long term to enable and develop capabilities.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: Are more details available on the plans for the training and mentorship framework?

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: How can TACs continue to help on this journey.?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Teo Ser Luck, you can do both your cuts.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Mr Chairman, MTI was very clear in strengthening the local enterprises and I believe they have a pyramid where most of the enterprises at the bottom were actually lower in revenue numbers – micro-enterprises and then small, medium and large.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: This is a very good pyramid to show.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Although we have over 200,000 SMEs in Singapore, every one is in its different places and most of them are actually micro enterprises.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: And I understand that MTI's strategy is quite clear.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Those who move the needles, there is a lot focus on them.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: And some of those who move the needles, they are actually large companies.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: And we have a Scale-up Programme within MTI or Enterprise (ESG) to help these companies to be strengthened.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: So, for example, what Mr Douglas Foo has mentioned about training the leaders, as well as after training the leaders, they make a transformation within a company and strengthen the company.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: But you might realise that a lot of the medium-sized companies, even to the smaller-sized companies, not micro enterprises yet, but smaller ones to the medium-sized ones, they have a lot of potential.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: But the medium enterprises and the small enterprises might have the innovation, technology, concepts and plans or very passionate and enthusiastic entrepreneurs or founders that run them that could potentially make them global.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: And I would like to speak more about the micro enterprises as well.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: For those who have potential, we can grow them.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: But you know that some of them in the heartlands who are micro enterprises may not have the chance at all.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: But these micro enterprises at the heartlands, we call them "heartland enterprises", they have both a commercial and also a social impact on our lives.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Having lived in a Housing and Development Board (HDB) estate for more than 25 years, there are a lot of the shops that I still visit today, and that personalised approach keeps them going.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Several of us continue to patronise those shops and they continue to be there.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: I know that the Ministry of National Development (MND) and MTI are trying to spruce up these heartland enterprises.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: One of the major things they do in the past few years was upgrading the hardware facilities, the surroundings, hopefully, to capture the foot traffic.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: But you know, it is not just the hardware that we should upgrade.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: It is about helping these heartland enterprises maybe about a centralised inventory planning, financial planning, product innovation.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: And some of these things actually matter – bringing them online and become more e-commerce focused.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: And this may help them to draw in more customers instead of looking at just the foot traffic because, if it is just the foot traffic, they compete directly with the heartland malls and their prices.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: So, they may not have a chance to position themselves.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, during this period of the COVID-19 outbreak, people are taking precautions and minimising contact by avoiding crowds where possible.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the Ministry provide the expertise and guide them towards any support grants so that they can serve more customers through this relatively new sales channel?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, there are many more people now who prefer to have their meals and groceries delivered to them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope the Ministry will take this opportunity to help more of our heartland enterprises move towards digitalisation.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I have three points for MTI's consideration regarding consumer matters.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This action of retailers taking advantage of consumers and profiteering during the COVID-19 outbreak is simply unacceptable.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: What else can MTI do to warn businesses that they should not profiteer and should not take advantage of consumers during uncertain times?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: CASE will be happy to continue working with MTI to educate and empower consumers to know more about their rights and to protect themselves from unscrupulous businesses.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Next, it was recently reported in the media that some consumers were cheated when they tried to buy face masks online via Carousell.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Last year, I asked MAS to work with the Association of Banks of Singapore (ABS) and credit card issuing banks to raise awareness of charge-back schemes.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And this will enable consumers to seek refund from their credit card banks if they encounter a dishonest online vendor.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: After all, banks that provide banking facilities for their merchants have a better knowledge and control over their commercial partners.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Before applying for an injunction, CCCS needs to conduct an investigation and take statements from consumers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The process is quite tedious and not all consumers will want to spend their personal time giving statements to CCCS and appearing in Court as witnesses.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Sometimes, if the consumer needs to be publicly identified as someone who was taken advantage of, the consumer may rather not be embarrassed.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I am of the view that consumers will be more forthcoming if they do not have to worry about having to go to Court all the time.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore has faced challenging economic situations triggered by disease outbreaks before – the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) in 2003 and the Hemagglutinin 1 and Neuraminidase 1 (H1N1).

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Through each episode, we internalised important lessons, strengthened our collective resilience and emerged stronger.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Today, the Coronavirus Disease of 2019 (COVID-19) is badly hurting our tourism and aviation sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Retail and food services have also been severely affected.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The disruption of supply chains has also slowed the recovery of the manufacturing sector, especially electronics.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The quantitative and qualitative impact of China’s slowdown and the potential of a global pandemic cannot be underestimated.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Many of us are concerned how the COVID-19 situation will affect our livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I want to reassure Singaporeans that the Government’s immediate priorities are to help our businesses stay afloat and to help our workers stay employed.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To this end, we have introduced a comprehensive set of relief measures in the Stabilisation and Support Package.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Measures like the Enhancement of the Enterprise Financing Scheme – SME Working Capital Loan will support businesses with cash flow issues that may arise in the short term.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Chairman, beyond the measures to address the immediate challenges ahead, we must also aspire to emerge stronger, be one of the first to recover and seize the new opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This Government is committed to not just the present, but also our future.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our most immediate task is to rejuvenate the tourism and related sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will also commit resources to support the upgrading of hotels and attractions during this period of lower activity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will anchor a strong pipeline of leisure and business events in the recovery and step up marketing efforts to reach new sources of tourists.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: International investors remain committed to Singapore as we forge ahead with plans to enhance our attractiveness as a tourism destination.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Large-scale tourism projects, such as the Integrated Resorts expansion, Sentosa-Brani Masterplan and rejuvenation of the Mandai precinct all continue to make good progress.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They will contribute to the growth of our tourism sector in the medium term.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Beyond tourism, we must also press on with our efforts to transform our economy for tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Teo Ser Luck and Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked about the Ministry of Trade and Industry's (MTI’s) plans for the longer term.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must prepare for two sets of long-term driving forces.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First, we must prepare for the reordering of global supply chains; technology, especially digital technologies; rising trade tensions and protectionism; and now domestic resilience to disease outbreaks have all added impetus to the reordering of the global supply chains.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: All companies, big and small, local and multinational, have to fundamentally re-examine the resilience of our supply chains.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Diversification of supplies, manpower sources and markets are not options but imperatives.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The ensuing contest to attract top investments and talent will be intense.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Developing countries with plentiful land and labour are cutting costs aggressively.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: More developed countries are poaching top executives and building their very own Smart Cities to rival Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development's (OECD's) Base Erosion and Profit Shifting initiative (BEPS 2.0) will also impact how countries compete for investments.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To differentiate ourselves, we can no longer rely on tax incentives alone.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Instead, Singapore must continually build real and new capabilities, augment our Singapore Core with global talent and find new ways to anchor key economic activities here.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are undergoing technological advancements in multiple fields – medical, robotics, artificial intelligence (AI) and energy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These are not just incremental shifts, but disruptive and discontinuous change.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The emergence of new technology provides us with new economic opportunities and challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Sectors in which we did not have a comparative advantage before, like agri-tech and new urban mobility solutions, are now emerging opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: On the flipside, technology is now challenging sectors which are well-established in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Banking is being disrupted by the rise of financial technology (FinTech).

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Some legal, consultancy and information technology (IT) services can now be delivered electronically across borders.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Whether we can win depends on two things.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Externally, whether we can extend and enhance our connections; internally, whether we can adapt our environment and businesses to the two forces of global supply chains being reordered and emerging technology.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In November last year, we concluded text-based negotiations for the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP).

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are also making progress in FTA negotiations with the Eurasian Economic Union, the South American Common Market (MERCOSUR) and the Pacific Alliance.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our FTAs have provided our businesses access to billions of consumers beyond Singapore’s shores by reducing tariffs and lowering non-tariff barriers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Having FTAs in different regions facilitates diversification and enables our businesses to capitalise on opportunities around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The benefit of each FTA goes far beyond our economic relations with the other party.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our FTAs enhance our ability to compete for investments as a network of 25.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Companies which operate in Singapore can use our FTAs to build up supply and value chains which are resilient to single-market disruptions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: At the same time, many companies also find it advantageous to access the Southeast Asia region and the world through Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This creates many opportunities for businesses in Singapore and allows them to create good job opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Leon Perera asked about the FTA negotiation process.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In order to achieve the best outcomes for Singapore, we consult and involve many different stakeholders, including trade associations, unions and business chambers, in the lead-up to the negotiations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Post FTA implementation, we continue to engage industry and regularly enhance our trade agreements, where possible.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For example, we upgraded our FTA with China to provide our businesses with new benefits like enhanced investment protection and greater access to China's legal, maritime and construction services sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We also upgraded our FTA with New Zealand last year, and now businesses can clear their goods through New Zealand Customs much faster.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We also adapt our trade agreements to the emergence of new technologies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For example, we have started work on Digital Economy Agreements (DEAs) as we call them.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Negotiations with other like-minded partners, including Australia, are also progressing well.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As we enhance our trade agreements, we must also help our companies to take advantage of them.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Douglas Foo, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Teo Ser Luck asked how we can do more to support businesses in seizing opportunities in the region and beyond.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Moving ahead, we will significantly strengthen our support to companies that want to go international, in five ways.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To better support companies which are new to internationalisation or are expanding into new markets, the grant cap will be raised to $100,000 per new market per company over the enhancement period.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We have also expanded the scope of eligible activities to include in-depth FTA consultancy services and support for additional overseas business development activities, such as the cost of deploying a staff overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This will encourage more Singapore companies to increase their market development and investment activities overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The enhancements will now cover new categories of expenses incurred for third-party consultancy and overseas business missions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Third, we will launch the Grow Digital initiative under the small and medium enterprises (SMEs) Go Digital programme to help SMEs grow their business overseas via both business-to-business (B2B) and business-to-consumer (B2C) digital channels to access new customers and markets.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For a start, the programme will focus on China, India and Southeast Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Minister S Iswaran will share more details at the Ministry of Communications and Information's (MCI's) Committee of Supply (COS) debate.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Fourth, we will work with the Singapore Business Federation (SBF) to launch the GlobalConnect@SBF in April.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: GlobalConnect will be an international advisory centre to provide dedicated market access support for companies new to internationalisation, with a focus on Southeast Asia and the emerging markets.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Fifth, we will increase the support levels for young Singaporeans under the Global Ready Talent (GRT) Programme so that more graduates can take on work opportunities abroad and gain exposure to Southeast Asia, China and India.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This will strengthen the pipeline of local talent to support businesses in expanding overseas in the medium to long term.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Teo Ser Luck will also be pleased to note that our suite of internationalisaton support goes beyond providing financial support.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We also focus on the facilitation of knowledge transfers to companies, as suggested by Mr Teo.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Through a network of overseas centres, Enterprise Singapore works closely with companies to provide advisory support and in-market assistance.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They also run frequent seminars to equip SMEs with essential knowledge to embark on their internationalisation journey.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To better understand the industry, we have been seconding Public Service officers to Trade Associations and Chambers (TACs) through the Local Enterprise and Association Development (LEAD) Programme.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These officers have been actively involved in helping the TACs spearhead new internationalisation projects for the industries and we will do more where we can to second more officers to the TACs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But they must be complemented by measures to strengthen ourselves internally, so that we can harness the two global trends to emerge stronger.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Specifically, we must emerge stronger through innovation, transformation and doing it together as an entire ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Public investment in research and innovation has grown over the last 25 years.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This puts us in a good position to harness the technological revolution and turn old constraints into new opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We have a small population, less than 1% of ASEAN.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, we leverage the advanced manufacturing sector to propel ourselves from a labour-intensive industry to one empowered by Industry 4.0 technologies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This has also allowed us to establish our niche in producing "high-mix, low-volume, high-quality and knowledge-intensive" products, entrenching our position in the global value chains.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, we leverage agri-food technologies to transcend both size and geography, producing high-value crops like strawberry and kale on this sunny island.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, we explore innovative solutions to transform waste into value-add products.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This has allowed us to couple environmental sustainability with economic prosperity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will also continue to drive the adoption of technologies through the Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs) and to seize new opportunities in emerging sectors, especially in the Deep Tech sector.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: My colleague, Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon, will elaborate.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The use of technology must be complemented by the transformation of business processes.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We recognise that not all enterprises are at the same stage of development.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But regardless of your stage of growth, you will have a fair chance to succeed.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will customise our assistance to our enterprises' needs and level of ambition.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For local enterprises with high growth potential, we will provide dedicated support to deepen their capabilities, enabling them to become leaders in their respective fields.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For smaller enterprises, we will enhance access to the wide array of enterprise-centric enablers, through channels like the SME Centres, the TACs and the GoBusiness platform.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For Heartland Enterprises, we will provide additional assistance through schemes like Heartland Enterprise Upgrading Programme (HEUP) so that they, too, can have a good shot at growth and expansion.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our assurance to all Singaporean business is this: so long as you have the drive and you have the ambition, we will partner you, as necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: My colleague, Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat, will elaborate on these schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Over the years, we have established a strong tripartite partnership amongst the Government, the TACs and the unions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As key touchpoints to businesses and workers, TACs and the unions help provide the Government with crucial ground sensing and feedback on key economic policies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Moving forward, we will do more to strengthen our partnership with TACs to drive industry transformation efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: My colleague Senior Parliamentary Secretary Tan Wu Meng will elaborate.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Chairman, we are committed to sharing the benefits of economic growth with all Singaporeans and improve their lives.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Desmond Choo asked about how efforts to grow the economy have translated into positive workers' outcome.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: When we grow the economic pie, we create good jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We also share the fruits of economic growth.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Economic growth is necessary to create good jobs for Singaporeans, but I must say this does not happen naturally.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The critical link between growth and jobs is skills.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Singaporeans must have the right skills to take on the jobs that growth creates.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Government has put in significant investments in our education and training systems over many years.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We now have strong pre-employment training (PET) and continuing education and training (CET) systems and our SkillsFuture movement, which are all well-regarded globally.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There are capability-building programmes to transfer overseas capabilities and expertise to our local workforce, such as the Capability Transfer Programme.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We have also placed strong emphasis on grooming local leaders within key sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In particular, the ASEAN Leadership Programme (ALP) will equip our business leaders with the knowledge and network to ride on the growth of Southeast Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: However, as Mr Saktiandi Supaat noted, employers must have the right mindset for these programmes to succeed.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They need to start investing in our local workers and to prevent an over-reliance on foreign employees.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Only then will we be able to improve the localisation over time.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Indeed, we must not and we must never be complacent.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Today, many have jobs that did not exist a mere decade ago.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are preparing for future jobs that do not yet exist now.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The rate of technological change will only quicken.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If we do not support our workers in refreshing and advancing their skills, not only will they lose employability over time, businesses will suffer, and our economy will lose its competitiveness.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are particularly aware of the concerns amongst our mid-career workers, those in their 40s and 50s.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Job security is of utmost importance to them.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They have significant financial commitments as they provide for their families, often with school-going children and retired parents.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Many of them have completed their formal education more than 20 years ago and they have moved on in their careers in one company or various, and may not have the opportunity to reskill and upskill.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Those who are employed now are worried if they will still have a job in the near future because of keen job competition and also the technological disruption.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Those who have been retrenched are worried if they can re-enter the workforce and find a job that matches their skillsets and pay expectations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Desmond Choo , Mr Henry Kwek and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked what more can be done to support mid-career workers in their 40s and 50s.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This needs to be done at the tripartite level – businesses offering more employment and upgrading opportunities; workers making an effort to reskill; and the Government supporting businesses and workers in their endeavours.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, all three parties must pull our weight together in order to get this done.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I will talk about the support for businesses in general.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
